difficultyReason: Classic correlation-causation flaw with two plausible trap answers. Students must distinguish between 'ignores a third factor' and 'reverses cause and effect,' both of which are live distractors.
stimulus: A hospital administrator noticed that patients who are visited frequently by family members tend to recover from surgery more quickly than those who receive few visits. The administrator concluded that family visits must speed up the surgical recovery process and recommended that the hospital expand visiting hours accordingly.
questionStem: The administrator's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all surgical patients based on the experience of only a small number of them

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two factors for a causal relationship between them

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider whether expanding visiting hours would be financially feasible for the hospital

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that whatever benefits some patients must benefit all patients equally

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that the speed of recovery is the most important measure of surgical success

explanations.correct: The administrator observes that frequent visits and faster recovery co-occur and immediately infers that the visits cause the recovery. But the correlation could reflect a third factor — e.g., patients in better overall health both recover faster and attract more visitors — or could even run the other way. Inferring causation from correlation alone is the central structural flaw.
explanations.A: Nothing in the stimulus indicates the sample was small; the administrator's observation is presented as a general pattern. This is a plausible-but-absent flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. The stimulus moves directly from 'tend to co-occur' to 'must speed up,' which is an unwarranted causal inference from a correlation.
explanations.C: Financial feasibility concerns the recommendation's practicality, not the logical validity of the causal reasoning. This is an accurate-but-harmless observation.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't claim uniform benefit; it makes a general causal claim. This misdescribes the argument's structure.
explanations.E: Speed of recovery is the metric observed, but the argument doesn't assert it is the most important metric. This is a peripheral observation, not the structural flaw.

difficultyReason: False dichotomy with a tempting trap answer that correctly identifies the flaw type but misdescribes its location in the argument. Students must verify which dichotomy the stimulus actually presents.
stimulus: City Councilor: Our city's budget shortfall can be addressed in only one of two ways: we either raise property taxes or we lay off municipal employees. Since laying off employees would devastate essential services, it is clear that we must raise property taxes.
questionStem: The reasoning in the councilor's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that raising property taxes will actually eliminate the budget shortfall

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that only two solutions to the budget shortfall are available

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that laying off some employees might not devastate essential services

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about fiscal policy based on emotional considerations rather than economic analysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that property tax increases and employee layoffs are mutually exclusive responses

explanations.correct: The councilor asserts there are exactly two options without justifying why other approaches — spending cuts, new revenue streams, federal grants, debt restructuring — are unavailable. Presenting an artificially narrow set of options without defending their exhaustiveness is a false dichotomy.
explanations.A: Whether taxes will fully close the shortfall is a separate concern; the argument's flaw is in the prior step of restricting the options. This is accurate but peripheral.
explanations.B: Correct. The councilor states the choice is between only two options without ruling out alternatives, which is the defining false-dichotomy move.
explanations.C: Even partial layoffs might be harmful; but this addresses the severity of one horn, not the false restriction of the dilemma to two horns.
explanations.D: Nothing in the stimulus signals that the councilor is appealing to emotion rather than reasoning; 'devastate essential services' is presented as a factual consequence. This misdescribes the argument.
explanations.E: The argument doesn't assume they're mutually exclusive — it frames them as the only options. The issue is exhaustiveness, not exclusivity, mirroring the trap from the mayor anchor.

difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient confusion in an economics context. One trap answer describes the flaw in the reverse direction; another plausibly describes a different but related logical error.
stimulus: Economist: Every thriving national economy has a stable currency. Clearly, then, if a country stabilizes its currency, its economy will thrive.
questionStem: The economist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a sample of national economies that may not be representative of all economies

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient for economic prosperity as though it were merely necessary for it

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary for economic prosperity as though it were sufficient for it

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to define what it means for an economy to be described as thriving

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about future economic conditions from evidence about past economic conditions

explanations.correct: The premise establishes that a stable currency is present in every thriving economy — making it a necessary condition (thriving → stable currency). The economist then concludes that having a stable currency guarantees a thriving economy, treating the necessary condition as if it were sufficient (stable currency → thriving). This is the classic necessary/sufficient confusion.
explanations.A: The stimulus presents a universal generalization ('every thriving economy'), not a sample-based inference. No sampling is involved.
explanations.B: This describes the flaw in reverse: the argument actually treats a necessary condition as sufficient, not a sufficient condition as necessary.
explanations.C: Correct. Stable currency is necessary (all thriving economies have it) but the economist concludes it is sufficient (having it produces thriving), which is unwarranted.
explanations.D: While 'thriving' could be vague, this is a peripheral concern and does not identify the structural logical error the argument commits.
explanations.E: The argument doesn't make a temporal claim about future versus past; it makes a conditional logical claim. This misdescribes the argument's structure.

difficultyReason: Ad hominem flaw clearly present but paired with a tempting trap that describes a real weakness (unsupported premise about credibility) rather than the structural error.
stimulus: Nutritionist: The senator's proposal to mandate nutrition labels on restaurant menus deserves no serious consideration. After all, the senator has accepted significant campaign contributions from the fast-food industry and therefore has a clear financial conflict of interest.
questionStem: The nutritionist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the senator's character rather than addressing the merits of the proposal itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without justification that campaign contributions always influence a legislator's policy positions

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that mandatory nutrition labeling might impose costs on restaurant owners

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about nutrition policy from a single case

choices.label: E
choices.text: presupposes that the nutritionist's own position is free of bias

explanations.correct: The nutritionist dismisses the proposal not by showing it is bad policy, but by pointing to the senator's financial ties. Whatever the senator's motives, the proposal's merits stand independently of who proposed it. This is an ad hominem (circumstantial) flaw.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument targets the senator's circumstances rather than engaging with whether mandatory nutrition labeling is a good or bad policy idea.
explanations.B: This identifies an unsupported premise in the argument (the link from contributions to influence), but the more fundamental structural flaw is that even if the senator is biased, the proposal could still be sound. B is a peripheral weakness, not the central error.
explanations.C: Restaurant costs are a separate policy consideration the argument never engages; this is accurate-but-harmless and doesn't identify the logical flaw.
explanations.D: No generalization across cases is made; the argument focuses on a single proposal. This misdescribes the argument.
explanations.E: The nutritionist's own bias is not raised in the stimulus; this imports an external consideration irrelevant to the stated reasoning.

difficultyReason: Overgeneralization from a potentially unrepresentative sample. The trap answers include a plausible correlation-causation error and an accurate-but-harmless criticism about methodology.
stimulus: A technology journalist surveyed software engineers at three large Silicon Valley firms and found that the majority preferred working remotely full-time. The journalist concluded that most software engineers in the country prefer remote work.
questionStem: The journalist's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes a preference for remote work for a demonstrated ability to be productive while working remotely

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a broad conclusion about software engineers generally from a sample that may not be representative of all software engineers

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider whether engineers at these firms were given a genuine choice about their work arrangements

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the majority preference within each firm as equivalent to a majority preference across all firms

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that the conditions that apply in Silicon Valley apply equally in all technology sectors

explanations.correct: The journalist surveys engineers at three large Silicon Valley firms — a geographically concentrated, industry-specific sample — and generalizes to all software engineers nationwide. Engineers at smaller firms, in different regions, or in non-tech-hub cities may have very different preferences. Drawing a broad conclusion from this restricted sample is the flaw.
explanations.A: The argument is about preferences, not productivity. Introducing productivity confuses the conclusion's content. This is a plausible-but-absent flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. Three large Silicon Valley firms are not representative of the full population of software engineers across the country, making the generalization unwarranted.
explanations.C: Whether the choice was genuine is a concern about the survey's internal validity, but the primary structural flaw is the unrepresentative sample, not the quality of the choice offered.
explanations.D: The argument draws a national conclusion, not a cross-firm aggregation error specifically. This misdescribes the precise move the journalist makes.
explanations.E: This is a reformulation of the unrepresentativeness concern but is narrower and less precisely captures the flaw than B, which covers geographic and firm-size dimensions together.

difficultyReason: Circular reasoning (question-begging) in an ethics context. The trap answer describes a real concern about the argument's premise but mistakes it for a different flaw type.
stimulus: Ethicist: Euthanasia must be morally wrong because deliberately ending a person's life is always an immoral act. And we know that deliberately ending a person's life is always immoral because euthanasia — which is a form of deliberately ending a life — is morally wrong.
questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a definition of euthanasia that is disputed by those who support the practice

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses the conclusion it is trying to establish as part of the support for that very conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider cases in which ending a life might prevent greater suffering

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a universal conclusion from a limited number of cases involving deliberate harm

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a moral intuition as though it were an established philosophical principle

explanations.correct: The ethicist argues that euthanasia is wrong because deliberately ending life is immoral, and then supports the claim that deliberately ending life is immoral by pointing to euthanasia being wrong. Each claim depends on the other, making the reasoning circular — the conclusion is embedded in the premises.
explanations.A: Whether euthanasia is contested is not relevant to the logical structure of the argument; the flaw is in how the premises relate to the conclusion, not in how the term is defined.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument is classically circular: euthanasia is wrong (conclusion) ← deliberately ending life is immoral (premise) ← euthanasia is wrong (conclusion reused as support).
explanations.C: This introduces a consequentialist consideration absent from the stimulus. While relevant to the broader debate, it does not identify the structural logical error in the argument as presented.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't enumerate cases; it makes a categorical claim. No sample-based inference occurs here.
explanations.E: Nothing in the stimulus suggests the claim is merely an intuition versus a principle; this description does not capture the circular structure.

difficultyReason: Scope shift / equivocation on a key term ('significant') in a law context. One trap describes a real but peripheral weakness; another reverses the direction of the logical error.
stimulus: Legal scholar: Any law that has a significant impact on commerce is subject to congressional oversight. The proposed environmental regulation would require companies to disclose their carbon emissions quarterly, which would certainly affect how companies allocate their reporting resources. Therefore, this regulation is subject to congressional oversight.
questionStem: The legal scholar's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient to trigger congressional oversight as though it were the only such condition

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that congressional oversight may itself be subject to legal challenge

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes without justification that affecting how companies allocate reporting resources constitutes a significant impact on commerce

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific regulation without examining the full text of the relevant statute

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that all environmental regulations have a significant impact on commerce

explanations.correct: The general rule requires a 'significant impact on commerce.' The scholar then points to an impact on 'reporting resources' — an administrative burden — and treats that as equivalent to a significant commercial impact without any justification for the equivalence. This is a scope shift: the term 'significant impact on commerce' in the premise is quietly replaced with a narrower, weaker effect in the application.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't claim that commercial impact is the only trigger for oversight; it simply applies that one trigger. This misdescribes the argument.
explanations.B: Whether oversight itself is legally challengeable is entirely external to the argument's logical structure. This is accurate-but-harmless.
explanations.C: Correct. The scholar slides from 'significant impact on commerce' to 'affects reporting resource allocation' without establishing that these are equivalent, which is the central gap.
explanations.D: Consulting statutory text is a legal practice concern, not a logical flaw. This is peripheral and does not describe the structural error.
explanations.E: The argument concerns only this specific regulation; it makes no general claim about all environmental regulations.

difficultyReason: Reversed causation flaw in an environmental science context. The trap answers include a correlation-causation variant and a false dichotomy, requiring the student to identify the specific direction of the causal error.
stimulus: Environmental researcher: In regions where the population of large predators has declined sharply, we observe significant increases in soil erosion. This demonstrates that the loss of large predators is causing the soil erosion in these regions.
questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it fails to consider the possibility that

choices.label: A
choices.text: soil erosion and predator population decline may both be caused by a third factor, such as habitat destruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: large predators may play no meaningful role in regulating the plant species that prevent erosion

choices.label: C
choices.text: the regions studied may not be representative of all regions experiencing predator decline

choices.label: D
choices.text: soil erosion rates may be influenced by seasonal weather patterns unrelated to predator populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: preventing soil erosion may require restoring predator populations to levels higher than those that previously existed

explanations.correct: The researcher observes that predator decline and soil erosion co-occur and concludes that one causes the other. But a third variable — such as large-scale habitat destruction — could independently reduce predator populations and destabilize the plant cover that prevents erosion. The researcher fails to rule out this common-cause explanation, making the causal inference unwarranted.
explanations.A: Correct. The existence of a common cause (habitat destruction, deforestation, drought) would explain the correlation without any direct causal link between predator decline and erosion.
explanations.B: This would challenge whether the proposed mechanism is plausible, but the flaw identified in the question stem is that the argument ignores alternative explanations for the observed correlation — not that the mechanism is biologically implausible.
explanations.C: Sample representativeness is a separate concern about generalizability, not about whether the causal inference from the observed data is valid.
explanations.D: Weather patterns could affect erosion rates, but this is a competing causal factor for erosion alone, not a common cause of both observed phenomena. It is a weaker version of the relevant flaw.
explanations.E: What level of predator restoration would be needed is a policy concern entirely outside the logical scope of the causal argument.

difficultyReason: Division fallacy (what is true of the whole treated as true of each part) in a linguistics/history context. The trap answers include an overgeneralization and a false dichotomy, both plausible on quick reading.
stimulus: Historian: The Roman Empire was extraordinarily successful at assimilating foreign cultures, incorporating diverse languages, religions, and customs into a cohesive imperial identity. Therefore, each Roman provincial administrator must have been skilled at managing cultural diversity.
questionStem: The historian's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an institution's policy from evidence about the attitudes of its individual members

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a characteristic true of a collective entity as necessarily true of each member of that entity

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that Roman assimilation may have involved coercion rather than voluntary cultural exchange

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that success in one domain of governance guarantees success in all domains

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases a historical conclusion on sources that may reflect imperial propaganda rather than objective fact

explanations.correct: The argument attributes a quality of the Roman Empire as a whole — skill at cultural assimilation — to each individual administrator within it. But a collective can achieve something through structural, systemic, or aggregate factors even when many individual members lack that quality. This is the division fallacy.
explanations.A: This describes the reverse of the actual move: the argument goes from collective to individual, not from individuals to institutional policy.
explanations.B: Correct. The historian infers from Rome's collective success at assimilation that each individual administrator must have been skilled — treating the group's property as necessarily a property of every member.
explanations.C: Whether assimilation was coercive is relevant to the empire's character but does not identify the structural logical flaw in the inference from collective to individual.
explanations.D: The argument stays within the domain of cultural management; it does not generalize across different domains of governance.
explanations.E: Source reliability is a historical methodology concern, not the logical flaw in the inference pattern itself.

difficultyReason: Equivocation on a key term ('original') in an arts/aesthetics context. Trap answers include a scope-shift description that almost fits and a plausible-but-absent ad hominem.
stimulus: Art critic: The works displayed in this gallery are truly original — no other artist has produced anything quite like them. And since original works are always more valuable than derivative ones, these works are clearly more valuable than anything else being sold at the art fair.
questionStem: The art critic's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses the term 'original' in two different senses: first to mean stylistically unique and then to mean aesthetically superior in market value

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without evidence that the works displayed are the only original works at the art fair

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that aesthetic value and market value are equivalent measures of worth

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that some derivative works may have sold for higher prices than original works in the past

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases its valuation on the critic's personal taste rather than on objective artistic standards

explanations.correct: The critic establishes that these works are original (no other artist has produced anything like them) and that original works are more valuable than derivative ones. But the conclusion — that these works are more valuable than anything else at the art fair — requires that nothing else at the art fair is original. The critic never establishes this, taking for granted that these are the only original works present.
explanations.A: The word 'original' is used consistently to mean 'stylistically unlike others' in both uses; the critic does not shift to a different meaning. This is the most tempting trap: it correctly identifies equivocation as a flaw type but mislocates it in this argument.
explanations.B: Correct. The general principle that original works beat derivative ones only lets the critic conclude these works are better than derivative works — not better than everything at the fair, unless everything else is derivative. That assumption is never supported.
explanations.C: The argument operates within a single domain of 'value' without conflating aesthetic and market value; this introduces a distinction absent from the stimulus.
explanations.D: Historical counterexamples would undermine the general premise, but the flaw identified here is in the argument's logical structure given its premises, not in whether those premises are empirically accurate.
explanations.E: Nothing in the stimulus indicates the critic's judgment is based on personal taste rather than on the stated criterion of originality. This is a plausible-but-absent ad hominem.
